title: Chapter 8 – The Yellow Paper Trade
html:
The first thing Lin Jian makes with Level Two is a pill.

He does it on the third night, in the granary, while Old Hu snores in the eastern wing and the forge coals tick as they cool. He has stolen nothing. Third Aunt keeps the cracked mortar and the leftover dust of her ginseng grinding in a jar on the pill-room windowsill, meaning to throw it on the herb beds, and a thumb's worth of pine resin and gray cliff moss go missing from her shelves so rarely that she will never notice. He sets the scraps on the workbench in a clean dish with a cup of spring water, and opens the panel.

```
[Pill Synthesis: Breath-Gathering Pill (Level 1)]
Recipe: observed (Lin Wenqing, 23 batches)
Inputs: spirit ginseng (powder, 0.4 portion), pine resin, north-cliff moss, spring water
Required Qi: 1.20
Projected purity: 96%
Begin? Y
```

One point two. More than half of everything he has.

The blue shimmer forms. The ginseng dust lifts out of the dish in a fine, spinning cloud, and the water rises to meet it, and the resin softens and runs like honey and threads itself through the spinning dust, and for perhaps twenty heartbeats he watches something that looks less like cooking and more like a small, patient storm. Then it collapses inward, and there is a click like a bead dropping into a bowl.

In the dish sits a pill. It is not dark brown. It is pale gold, the color of new straw, and it is perfectly round, and it smells of pine and rain.

```
[Synthesis Complete]
Product: Breath-Gathering Pill (Level 1)
Purity: 96.2%
Note: Active fraction 3.1× Lin Wenqing's average.
```

He swallows it at once, before he can think better of it, and sits down cross-legged on the cold flagstones, and begins the wheel.

It is like opening a sluice gate. The cold Qi does not trickle into his dantian; it pours. For the space of an hour he feels the five threads of his root running full, water, wood, fire, earth, metal, one after another, so fast and so smooth that the wheel turns of its own accord and he only has to keep his hands on it. When it ends, he is soaked with sweat and his head is ringing.

```
Host Qi Reserve: 2.31 / 2.80 (Qi Refining, Layer 2)
Gain from single pill: +0.41 (≈ 20 nights of unassisted cultivation)
```

Twenty nights in one.

He sits in the dark a long time after that, doing arithmetic. One pill costs him a little more than a day of cultivation to make and gives him twenty days back. The limit is not the pill. The limit is how many pills a boy can make without anyone noticing that the pill room's scraps are disappearing.

He decides on one a week. Then he goes to bed, and lies awake, and feels the new Qi turning slowly in his belly like a wheel that has finally found its axle.

\ \ \*

The second thing he makes is the bath.

Every dawn, before Old Hu wakes, he takes one cup of the crude decoction from the iron pot and refines it on the workbench: the iron-root sap drawn out of the fibers, the pepper oils freed from the bark, the bone ash broken down so fine that it disappears into the water like milk. The cost is small, a third of a point of Qi. The result is a cup of liquid the color of strong tea that smells like a burning forest and makes his eyes water from across the room.

```
[Separation / Refinement: Body Tempering Decoction]
Iron-root extraction: 18% → 94%
Pepper bark extraction: 34% → 97%
Bone ash: suspended (particle size 1/400 original)
Effectiveness: ×5.2 (estimated)
```

He stirs the cup into the tub before Old Hu fills it.

The first morning he climbs into it, he nearly screams. It is not five times the pain. It feels like fifty. But when he climbs out an hour later and looks at his arms, the red flush on his skin has a faint coppery sheen under it, like the patina on old bronze, and when he presses a fingernail into his forearm the skin pushes back.

Old Hu, emptying the tub, stops and sniffs the dregs.

Then he looks at the clay cup on the workbench, still stained dark at the bottom. Then at Lin Jian.

He says nothing. He empties the tub.

The next morning, beside the iron pot, there is a bigger cup.

\ \ \*

He tests himself in secret, too.

It is not something he plans. It is something that happens, the way a question happens. He has spent months practicing Earthen Rampart and Cloudstep on a threshing floor, against pine needles that do not fight back. He has no idea whether either of them is any use against something that does. And everything he has learned in two lives says that you do not trust a design until you have tested it under load.

So on a gray morning in late summer, when his mother has gone to Willow Ford with Third Aunt and Lin Feng is at spear practice and Old Hu is too hungover to notice anything, he puts his father's talisman case inside his short robe, buckles on the bracer, and slips out of the eastern postern while the guards are changing.

He does not go far. The stream at the edge of the outer forest, an hour's walk, the place where his mother showed him the blood-stop grass. He tells himself he will go no farther. He keeps that promise.

The thing he finds by the water is a stone badger.

It is a first-rank beast, low and broad, the size of a large dog, with a pelt of coarse gray hair over a hide studded with nodules of something like flint. It is digging for grubs in the bank. When it smells him, it lifts its head, and its small, red-rimmed eyes fix on him, and it makes a sound like gravel in a bucket.

Stone badgers, his mother said, are first rank, low tier, and do not run.

It charges.

He has perhaps two heartbeats. He spends the first one raising a ridge. Not in front of it, where it would simply go over or through. Diagonally, a shin-high lip of earth at an angle across its path, so that its forefeet hit the slope and skid sideways. He spends the second one on Cloudstep, wood and then metal, a vortex the height of his knee spinning up exactly where its hindquarters are, as its front end is already sliding.

The badger turns over.

Not gracefully. It rolls onto its back in the mud at the stream's edge, all four stubby legs pumping at the air, its soft, hairless belly showing pale and pink.

He has not planned the third heartbeat. He stands there staring at the upturned badger, and it rights itself with a furious snort, and he realizes that he has no way to hurt it at all. His Qi is nearly gone. He has no blade. His father's Flame-Burst is in the case in his short robe, and he will not waste it on a badger.

The badger shakes the mud out of its ears and looks at him, and comes again.

This time he does not try to stop it. He raises his forearm, and drives everything that is left in him into the skin, the Ironhide Art, and the bracer flares as he barks the word. A shell of pale light flickers into being around him. The badger's flint-studded head smashes into it with a crack like a hammer on a pot, and the shell holds for exactly as long as Old Hu promised it would, and then breaks, and the badger's momentum carries it into his forearm.

It hurts. It hurts a great deal. But the skin does not split, and the bone does not break, and the badger, which has never in its life bitten something that did not give, lets go and backs up two steps and looks at him with what is unmistakably surprise.

Then it turns around and waddles off into the ferns, as if it has decided he is not worth the trouble.

Lin Jian sits down in the mud and examines his arm. A bruise the size of his palm, already purple. A row of shallow dents where the flint nodules hit. No blood.

He casts the Ward Art on it, one element at a time, and watches the bruise fade from purple to yellow, and laughs, out loud, alone by the stream, for the first time in this life.

A ridge turns it, he thinks. Wind flips it. The bracer slows it. The skin holds. Not one of them alone would have done anything against a beast that weighs three times what he does. Together, in the right order, they turned it over and sent it home.

That is what a five-element root has. Not power. Order.

He is home before noon. His mother, coming back from Willow Ford that evening, looks at the mud dried on the cuffs of his leggings, and at the faint yellow ghost of a bruise on his forearm, and does not ask. But that night, when he begins the wheel, she does not sit by the door. She sits beside him on the floor, close enough to touch, and stays there until dawn.

\ \ \*

The paper begins with a sentence in an account book.

"Talisman losses this quarter," Second Uncle reads at the summer council, "sixty-one parts in a hundred. Wenyuan's hand is, regrettably, not improving."

His father says nothing. His left hand lies on his knee, trembling.

Lin Jian, who has been watching his father draw for five years, knows that this is not true. The willow pills have done more for the tremor than anyone has noticed. And he knows something else, because two years ago, at the age of four, he scanned a blank sheet of the family's talisman paper while his father was at dinner, and the blueprint has been sitting in his library ever since.

```
[Blueprint: Talisman Paper (Lin household, current)]
Fiber: bamboo / mulberry blend, poorly beaten
Density: uneven (variance 34%)
Sizing: patchy
Note: Qi conduction failure likely at density gaps.
```

And a few drops of his father's ink, scanned the same week.

```
[Blueprint: Talisman Ink (Lin household, current)]
Cinnabar, pine soot, hide glue, dried first-rank beast blood
Grit content: 4% (coarse)
Note: Particulate interrupts conductive lines.
```

He has thought about it for two years. Now, at Level Two, he can do something about it. But a five-element root boy who suddenly produces perfect paper is a wonder, and wonders are watched.

So he goes to Old Hu.

"I want to make paper," he says, in the granary, the next afternoon.

Old Hu, who is filing the teeth of a saw, does not look up. "Paper."

"For Father's talismans. It's the paper. Not his hand. The paper's lumpy, so the ink sits thick in some places and thin in others, and where it's thin, the Qi breaks." He hesitates. "Like a crack in a blade. You can't see it, but it's there."

Old Hu stops filing.

"And the ink has sand in it," Lin Jian says. "Little bits. They break the lines too."

The old refiner sets down the file and looks at him for a long time.

"And you want me to do what, exactly?"

"Nothing," says Lin Jian. "I'll do it. I want you to not lie. Just don't say anything, when people ask who made it."

Old Hu considers this. "That's the wall," he says.

"That's the wall."

"Hm." He picks up the file again. "What do you need?"

\ \ \*

What he needs, it turns out, is a machine.

Paper in this world is made the way it has been made for a thousand years: fibers soaked in a vat, pounded by hand with wooden mallets for days until they separate, then lifted out on a bamboo screen in a thin sheet and pressed and dried. The pounding is the problem. A tired servant with a mallet beats some fibers to a pulp and leaves others whole. The sheet comes out lumpy.

In his first life, the problem was solved four hundred years ago by a Dutch machine called a Hollander beater: a heavy roller studded with metal bars, turning in an oval trough, driven by a waterwheel, that beats fiber evenly for as long as you let it run.

He draws it for Old Hu on the granary floor with a stick of charcoal.

The trough, an oval channel like a racetrack. The roller, a log with iron bars set along its length. A bedplate under it, ridged to match. The waterwheel, which can sit in the runoff channel that already runs along the east wall to carry rainwater off the courtyard. The gears to step the speed up, wooden pegs on wooden wheels.

Old Hu looks at the drawing for a long time.

"Where," he says finally, "did you see this?"

"I didn't. I thought of it." Which is, in a sense, true. He is thinking of it right now.

Old Hu looks at the drawing again. "The gears are wrong," he says at last. "Those teeth will shear in a week. Make them wider at the root." He rubs out a gear with his boot and redraws it with the stick, faster and surer than Lin Jian could. "And the roller needs to be cedar. Pine will warp in the wet."

It takes them six weeks.

Fourth Uncle's guards fell a cedar on the north slope and drag it down to the courtyard with ropes and a pair of oxen. Old Hu forges forty iron bars for the roller, and the bedplate, and the axle. Lin Jian carves gear teeth until his hands blister, and heals the blisters with the Ward Art, and carves more. Fourth Uncle digs out the runoff channel and lines it with stone. Lin Feng, who pretends to have no interest at all, comes every evening and helps carry the heavy pieces, and asks no questions, and on the night the waterwheel first turns, he stands beside his brother in the dark and watches the roller begin to churn the white mash in the trough, and says, "Huh," which from Lin Feng is high praise.

Lin Hu, wandering past one afternoon while it is half built, kicks a loose stone into the trough to see what will happen. It jams the roller, and snaps a gear tooth, and costs them a day. That evening, by sheer coincidence, Old Hu drops a hammer on Lin Hu's foot while walking past him in the courtyard. Lin Hu limps for three days. Old Hu apologizes at great length and with no sign of remorse at all.

The first sheets come off the screen in late autumn. Lin Jian holds one up to the light from the granary door.

It is thin, almost translucent. Even. The light comes through it in a single smooth glow, with no dark patches and no bright ones. There is no interface in it. Every fiber was beaten by a cedar log turning in a trough of water, and pressed by a screw press Old Hu built from an old oil mill, and dried on boards in the sun. It is simply good paper, made by a good method.

The ink is different.

He refines that one alone, at night, while Old Hu drinks with Grandfather on the bench outside the main hall, as he has taken to doing most evenings. A pot of his father's ink, carried up from the desk on the pretext of grinding a fresh batch. Six tenths of a point of Qi.

```
[Separation / Refinement: Talisman Ink]
Grit removed: 99.6%
Cinnabar particle size: reduced 70%, uniform
Pine soot: retained
Beast blood: retained, dispersed
Result: Talisman Ink (Refined)
```

When he pours it back into his father's ink stone, it lies there like a pool of liquid lacquer, glossy and perfectly smooth, and catches the lamplight.

\ \ \*

His father tests the paper on a Mirror Guard.

He draws ten of them at his desk, by lamplight, with the household's usual ink, which Lin Jian has quietly replaced. He draws them exactly as he has drawn ten thousand others, his left hand braced against his right, his lips moving as he counts the strokes. When he finishes the tenth, he sets down the brush and stares at the row of slips drying on the desk.

None of them has crumbled.

He picks up the first, takes it out into the courtyard, tears it, and says "guard." A shell of gold light blooms around him, bright and solid. He counts. Five breaths. Six. Seven. Eight. It is still there.

He tears the next. And the next.

Nine of the ten hold for eight breaths or longer. The tenth fails at five.

His father stands in the courtyard in the gold light of his own talismans with his mouth open, and then he begins to laugh, and then he turns away so no one can see his face.

"It was the paper," he says, to nobody. "All these years. It was the paper."

That night, Lin Jian takes the tenth slip, the one that failed at five breaths, from the waste basket under his father's desk, and scans it.

He has scanned talismans before. He has never scanned one that he knew to be good paper and good ink, so that whatever is wrong with it must be wrong with the drawing itself. And this time the panel does something it has never done.

```
[Scan: Mirror Guard Talisman (Mortal Grade, spent)]
Circuit trace: reconstructed
— Input node (activation word) → 9 primary strokes → closure ring
— Fault: stroke 14 overlaps stroke 9 at the lower curl; current splits; 38% loss
Note: Inscription can be read as a Qi circuit. Optimization possible.
```

A diagram unfolds across his vision: the talisman's characters, not as ink, but as lines of light, with the Qi flowing through them like current through a wire. Most of it runs clean. But at the lower curl of the ninth character, where his father's tired hand always closes the loop a little too early, the line doubles back across itself, and the current splits and pools there and bleeds away.

He cannot tell his father that. He cannot tell anyone that.

So the next evening, when his father is drawing again, he sits on the floor beside the desk with his chin on his knees, watching, the way he has watched since he could crawl. When his father reaches the lower curl of the ninth character, he says, sleepily, "The ink always goes fat there."

His father pauses. "Where?"

"There. Where you go round. It goes fat and shiny. Like a puddle."

His father looks at the curl for a long moment. Then, on the next slip, he draws the ninth character with the lower curl last, after the stroke that crosses it, instead of before.

It holds for eleven breaths.

He does not say anything. He only looks at his son for a while, thoughtfully, and then goes back to drawing, and draws every Mirror Guard that way from then on.

\ \ \*

By midwinter, the Lin talismans are the talk of Willow Ford.

Mirror Guards that last a whole minute. Flame-Bursts that drive a thornback boar off a farmer's field. Fire Starters that catch on the first word, every time. Water slips that call enough rain to soak a whole terrace. The shop sells out within a week of each delivery, then within four days, then within two. Father trains two servants to work the press and the screens. Fourth Uncle's guards carry Mirror Guards in their belts on patrol. Third Aunt's herb beds have never been so green.

The Zhao shop across the square from the Lin shop cuts its prices again. It does not help.

And everyone on Green Pine Hill knows exactly who to thank.

"The refiner," they say in the village. "The one-armed refiner from the islands. He brought some method with him from the Eastern Sea." When anyone asks Old Hu about it directly, he grunts and says, "I build machines," and goes back to his forge, which is not a lie.

Old Hu gives Lin Jian his hammer on the first day of winter.

He does it without ceremony, as he does everything. He simply takes the small hammer with the hickory handle down from its place of honor at the center of the rack and holds it out.

"Thirty baskets before noon," he says. "Every day this week. My master gave me this when I made thirty." He pushes it into Lin Jian's hand. "Don't lose it."

Lin Jian looks down at the hammer. At the worn hickory, smooth as ivory. At the tiny mark on the cheek of the head, so faint he can barely see it: a hammer over three curved lines, like waves.

"Your master's mark?"

Old Hu is quiet for a moment. "His. Then mine. Then nobody's." He turns back to the forge. "Go carry gravel."

\ \ \*

In the deep of the winter, on a night when snow lies on the roofs and the whole hill is silent, Lin Jian reaches the third layer of Qi Refining.

It comes without warning, in the middle of the wheel, with the fourth of his gold pills still warm in his belly: a pressure, a crack, and then a sense of space, as if a room he has been living in has suddenly doubled in size.

```
[Host Status Update]
Qi Refining: Layer 3
Host Qi Reserve: 2.94 / 4.10
Channels opened: chest (6 / 6), back (2 / 8)
Five-Gate Wheel efficiency: 24%
```

Lin Feng took two years to go from the second layer to the third. Lin Hu took nearly three.

His mother, beside him on the floor, opens her eyes.

"Three," he says, very quietly.

She looks at him for a long time. Then she reaches out and lays her hand flat against his chest, over his heart, as if she is checking that it is still beating at the right speed.

"Not until spring," she says. "In the courtyard, you're still on your first layer. Next summer, your second. You're slow. Do you understand? You're the slowest child on this hill."

"Yes, Mother."

"Good." She takes her hand away. "Slow children live."

\ \ \*

The autumn tribute that year goes smoothly. For the first time in Lin Jian's memory, the treasury holds more than it needs.

At the council in the main hall, Second Uncle stands with his account book open and reads in his warm, rounded voice: "Shop income this season, seventy-two low-grade stones. Last autumn, forty. A remarkable improvement, thanks to our guest elder's methods." He bows toward Old Hu, who ignores him. "With the tribute paid, the treasury stands at three hundred and forty-one. A little to spare, for once."

Murmurs of approval around the table. Fourth Uncle smiles. Third Aunt nods. Even his father looks pleased.

Lin Jian, behind the folding screen in the corner with his eye to the torn third hinge, is not smiling.

He has been counting. He has counted every box of talismans that has gone down the hill to Willow Ford since midsummer, because he has watched every one of them leave from the granary door. He knows the price of each kind, because he has heard Old Fang, the shop's manager, shout it at customers through the window on the one occasion he has been to town. He knows how fast they sell, because the delivery boys complain about it at dinner.

His number is not seventy-two. It is somewhere around a hundred and twenty.

Fifty stones are missing. From one season.

He looks through the torn hinge at his grandfather.

Lin Zhenshan is sitting very still in the Patriarch's chair. His face shows nothing at all. His eyes are on his second son, resting there quietly, the way they might rest on a column of figures that does not quite add up.

The old man can count too.
